chapter: Race, revival and New Orleans jazz
title: White and Black musicians in early jazz; Raymond Burke
summary: Hug echoes Nick LaRocca on white musicians' role, and agrees Raymond Burke deserves more recognition than George Lewis.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I think this brings to mind something else. It's kind of a confused tradition in New Orleans that's been brought up that the glorification of the older musicians by critics and by fans has often overemphasized the older Negro musicians. I think we had some rabid white musicians who'd complain about this like Nick Garaka in kind of extreme terms and it's been sort of a cluttered image that's been presented to the public. You as a person who understudied the earlier jazz musicians, colored and white, might be able to throw some light on this. Do you think that the revival at Preservation Hall and thereabouts is distorted, overemphasized, let's say, underplaying the role of the white musicians who were important in the beginnings of jazz?

Well, I'll put it the way Nick LaRocca put it, as you say. I think that the jazz music belongs to New Orleans. You hate to get into something where you say which was better, was the colored music better or the white jazz music better? I think that stuff stuff

music had its place where they had the marching bands, which was a definite, a particular style of New Orleans, which I think belonged entirely, mostly, to the to the to the colored people. However, I do believe this, that the white musicians brought jazz to a higher level, to a higher standard, in when they brought it to New York. For instance, Nick LaRocca always said this, that that when they went to New York with their band, they played a different type of jazz. In fact, if you listen to it, if you listen to Dixieland One Step and That's A Plenty, and the type of tunes that the original Dixieland jazz band made, it's entirely different from the style of music that the marching bands did. Now of course I'm not trying to get into any controversy as to which was better or which was worse, but I do say this, that a lot of people had neglected the white part of this music, thinking that the Negro music was the only type of music, but I don't believe that it was. Okay. Of course I might get on for this.

I think you have a good point, because look, for example, at the reputation, commercially speaking of George Lewis and Raymond Burke. Raymond in his own way is, seems to me, is fully great a jazz musician as George is.
Well, I think every bit, every bit, I would even go so far as to say that I think even greater in some respects.
Right. But George is, worldwide, I think George is better known. He's better known, that's right.
There's a New Orleans cult who knows Raymond, but it seems to be limited to those who have been here and have heard him, and who have truly an intensive view into the New Orleans scene.
If you get to work with Raymond Burke and get to know how he plays, you know that he is really outstanding, and I don't think that, well, I mean, there's not many that can come up to him.
